about: Written by the /syllabus skill in Claude Code (.claude/skills/syllabus/SKILL.md). Do not edit by hand: run /syllabus.

teaches: A radius is a segment from the centre to the circle; a diameter is a chord through the centre, two radii end to end.
A chord is a segment joining two points of the circle; a secant is a line crossing the circle twice.
A tangent is a line that touches the circle at exactly one point.
An arc is a piece of the circle; two points split it into a minor and a major arc.
A sector is the region between two radii and their arc; a circular segment is the region between a chord and its arc.
The circumference of every circle is the same number of diameters long, and that number is $\pi \approx 3.14$.
$C = \pi d = 2\pi r$.
Cutting a disc into wedges and laying them alternately up and down approaches a rectangle $\pi r$ by $r$.
The area of a circle is $A = \pi r^2$.
Of all shapes with a given perimeter, the circle encloses the most area; it holds $\frac{4}{\pi} \approx 1.27$ times as much as a square with the same perimeter.
When two circles touch externally, the point of contact lies on the line of centres and $d = r_A + r_B$.
When one circle touches another from inside, $d = |r_A - r_B|$.
For three mutually externally tangent circles, each side of the triangle of centres is the sum of two radii.
Then $r_A = \tfrac12(AB + AC - BC)$.
An angle measures the fraction of a full turn a ray has swept.
Angles are named acute, right ($90^\circ$), obtuse, straight ($180^\circ$) or reflex.
A full turn is $360^\circ$ or $2\pi$ radians; to convert degrees to radians multiply by $\frac{2\pi}{360^\circ}$.
A degree splits into $60$ minutes and a minute into $60$ seconds, so $20.5^\circ = 20^\circ\,30'$.
The angle between two rays from a common vertex is measured in degrees.
An angle is acute below $90^\circ$, right at $90^\circ$ and obtuse between $90^\circ$ and $180^\circ$.
Two angles side by side along a straight line are supplementary: $\alpha + \beta = 180^\circ$.
Two angles are complementary when they add to $90^\circ$.
Where two lines cross, the vertical (opposite) angles are equal, because each is $180^\circ$ minus the same neighbour.
When a transversal crosses two parallel lines, corresponding angles are equal.
Alternate interior angles are equal.
Same-side interior angles add to $180^\circ$.
Conversely, if a transversal makes equal corresponding or alternate interior angles, or supplementary same-side angles, the two lines are parallel.
The angles of any triangle add to $180^\circ$: $\alpha + \beta + \gamma = 180^\circ$.
Proof: draw the parallel to $AB$ through $C$; alternate interior angles carry $\alpha$ and $\beta$ up to $C$, where the three angles fill a straight line.
An exterior angle of a triangle is formed by extending one side past a vertex.
An exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior angles far from it: $\delta = \alpha + \beta$.
The three exterior angles of a triangle, one at each vertex, add to $360^\circ$.
The measure of an arc is its central angle $\theta$, independent of the radius.
Arc length is $r\theta$ with $\theta$ in radians; at one radian the arc is as long as the radius.
Sector area is $\frac{\theta}{2\pi} \cdot \pi r^2 = \tfrac12 r^2\theta$.
A circular segment's area is the sector minus triangle $AOB$, or plus the triangle when the arc is more than a half turn.
An inscribed angle is half the central angle standing on the same arc: $\angle AOB = 2\angle APB$.
Proof: the diameter through $P$ makes two isosceles triangles of radii, whose exterior angles at $O$ are $2\alpha$ and $2\beta$; add or subtract depending on which side the diameter falls.
All inscribed angles standing on the same arc from the same side are equal.
An angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle: if $AB$ is a diameter, $\angle APB = 90^\circ$.
Conversely, the hypotenuse of a right triangle is a diameter of its circumcircle, so its midpoint is equally far from all three vertices.
When two chords cross inside a circle, the angle between them is half the sum of the arcs cut off by that angle and its vertical angle.
$\angle AEC = \tfrac12(\text{arc } AC + \text{arc } BD)$, proved by joining $AD$ and using inscribed angles and the exterior angle of triangle $AED$.
The angle between two secants from an outside point is half the far arc minus half the near arc: $\angle P = \tfrac12(\text{arc } BD - \text{arc } AC)$.
Proof: join $BC$; the exterior angle $\angle BCD$ of triangle $PBC$ equals $\angle P + \angle PBC$, and both are inscribed angles.
The same rule holds when one or both secants become tangents.
A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of tangency: $OT \perp TS$.
The angle between a tangent and a chord through the point of tangency is half the arc it cuts off.
So the tangent–chord angle equals any inscribed angle standing on that arc from the other side.
On the other side of the chord the tangent makes the supplement, half the arc on that side.
A triangle is acute when all three angles are less than $90^\circ$.
A triangle is right when one angle is exactly $90^\circ$.
A triangle is obtuse when one angle is greater than $90^\circ$.
A triangle can have at most one obtuse angle.
An equilateral triangle has three equal sides, at any size.
Each angle of an equilateral triangle is $60^\circ$, because the three equal angles share $180^\circ$.
An isosceles triangle has two equal sides, the legs, on either side of the apex; the third side is the base.
In an isosceles triangle the two base angles are equal.
A scalene triangle has no two sides equal.
In any triangle each side faces an angle, and the longest side faces the largest angle.
The perimeter of a triangle is the sum of its sides, $p = a + b + c$.
The semiperimeter is half the perimeter, $s = \frac{p}{2}$.
A median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.
The three medians of a triangle meet at a single point, the centroid $G$.
An angle bisector of a triangle runs from a vertex to the opposite side and splits the angle at that vertex into two equal angles.
Every point on the bisector of an angle is equally far from the angle's two sides, and every point equally far from both sides lies on the bisector.
The three angle bisectors of a triangle meet at a single point $I$, the incenter.
The incenter $I$ is the same distance $r$ from all three sides.
The circle with centre $I$ and radius $r$ touches all three sides, each at the foot of the perpendicular from $I$: the incircle.
Every point $P$ on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$ has $PA = PB$, and every point with $PA = PB$ lies on it.
The perpendicular bisectors of the three sides of a triangle meet at a single point $O$, the circumcenter.
The circle with centre $O$ and radius $R = OA = OB = OC$ passes through all three vertices: the circumcircle.
$O$ lies inside an acute triangle, on the hypotenuse of a right triangle, and outside an obtuse triangle.
In a right triangle $O$ is the midpoint of the hypotenuse, so the median to the hypotenuse equals $R = \tfrac{c}{2}$.
An altitude $h$ runs from a vertex perpendicular to the line through the opposite side.
In an obtuse triangle the altitudes from the two acute vertices land on the extensions of the opposite sides, outside the triangle.
The three altitudes meet at a single point, the orthocenter $H$.
$H$ is inside an acute triangle, at the right-angle vertex of a right triangle, and outside an obtuse triangle.
In any triangle each side is less than the sum of the other two: $a + b > c$, $b + c > a$ and $c + a > b$.
When one side exactly equals the sum of the other two, the triangle collapses into a straight line.
In a right triangle with legs $a$ and $b$ and hypotenuse $c$, $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$.
Proof: four copies of the triangle inside a square of side $a + b$ leave either the squares $a^2$ and $b^2$ or the one square $c^2$ uncovered, so $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$.
The two acute angles of a right triangle add up to $90^\circ$.
Four copies of a right triangle fit inside the square on its hypotenuse, leaving a square hole of side $|a - b|$.
So $c^2 = 4 \cdot \tfrac12 ab + (a - b)^2 = a^2 + b^2$, a second proof of the Pythagorean theorem.
The distance between two points is the hypotenuse $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ of the right triangle whose legs are their horizontal and vertical separations.
With an altitude $h$ from $A$ meeting line $BC$ at $D$ and $CD = x$, $c^2 = a^2 + b^2 \pm 2ax$.
If the angle at $C$ is obtuse then $c^2 > a^2 + b^2$; if it is acute then $c^2 < a^2 + b^2$.
Converse of Pythagoras: if the sides of a triangle satisfy $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$, the angle opposite $c$ is a right angle.
A Pythagorean triple is three whole numbers $(a, b, c)$ with $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$; usually $c = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ is not whole.
Multiplying every side of a right triangle by $n$ gives another right triangle, since $(na)^2 + (nb)^2 = (nc)^2$.
SSS: three sides fix a single triangle, up to its mirror image.
SAS: two sides and the angle between them fix a single triangle.
ASA: two angles and the side between them fix a single triangle.
SSA is not a congruence test: two sides and an angle not between them can give two different triangles.
AAS: two angles and a side not between them fix a triangle, since the third angle is $180^\circ$ minus the other two, which reduces it to ASA.
LL: two right triangles with equal legs are congruent, by SAS with the right angle between the legs.
SA: two right triangles with one equal side and one equal acute angle are congruent, since the last angle is $90^\circ - \beta$ and ASA applies.
HL: two right triangles with equal hypotenuses and one equal leg are congruent, since the other leg is $\sqrt{c^2 - a^2}$; this case of SSA works only because of the right angle.
If $AB = AC$, the base angles are equal: $\angle B = \angle C$ (the altitude from $A$ gives two right triangles congruent by HL).
Conversely, if $\angle B = \angle C$, then $AB = AC$ (the same two right triangles are congruent by SA).
In a triangle, equal sides and equal base angles always come together.
The radius through the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to the chord (triangles $OMA$ and $OMB$ are congruent by SSS).
A radius perpendicular to a chord bisects it (triangles $OMA$ and $OMB$ are congruent by HL).
Equal chords subtend equal central angles, and so cut off equal arcs.
Right triangles sharing an acute angle $\theta$ have the same angles $90^\circ$, $\theta$, $90^\circ - \theta$, and so are similar.
In similar triangles, the ratios of corresponding sides are equal, whatever the size.
The ratios $\frac{\text{opp}}{\text{hyp}}$, $\frac{\text{adj}}{\text{hyp}}$ and $\frac{\text{opp}}{\text{adj}}$ of a right triangle depend on the angle $\theta$ alone.
AA: two triangles with two pairs of equal angles are similar, and all three side ratios agree.
A line parallel to one side of a triangle cuts off a smaller triangle similar to it.

SAS similarity: two pairs of sides in the same ratio with the included angle equal make the triangles similar; for $\triangle ADE$ in $\triangle ABC$, $\tfrac{AD}{AB} = \tfrac{AE}{AC}$ exactly when $DE \parallel BC$.
SSS similarity: three pairs of sides in one ratio $k$ force equal angles.
Midsegment theorem: the segment joining the midpoints of two sides is parallel to the third side and half as long, $DE = \tfrac12 BC$.
The altitude to the hypotenuse of a right triangle splits it into two right triangles, each similar to the whole: $\triangle ACD \sim \triangle CBD \sim \triangle ABC$ by AA.
Geometric mean theorem: the altitude $h$ and the hypotenuse segments $p$, $q$ satisfy $h^2 = pq$.
Each leg is the geometric mean of the hypotenuse and its adjacent segment: $b^2 = cp$ and $a^2 = cq$.
Adding $a^2 = cq$ and $b^2 = cp$ gives a proof of $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$.
Angle bisector theorem: if $AX$ bisects angle $A$ of triangle $ABC$ with $X$ on $BC$, then $\dfrac{BX}{XC} = \dfrac{AB}{AC}$.
Proof: the line through $B$ parallel to $AC$ meets the extended bisector at $E$; alternate angles make $ABE$ isosceles with $BE = AB$, and $\triangle AXC \sim \triangle EXB$ by AA.
To find a ratio of lengths, draw a parallel to create similar triangles.
In a right triangle, $\sin = \frac{\text{opp}}{\text{hyp}}$, $\cos = \frac{\text{adj}}{\text{hyp}}$, $\tan = \frac{\text{opp}}{\text{adj}}$.
Their reciprocals are $\csc = \frac{1}{\sin}$, $\sec = \frac{1}{\cos}$ and $\cot = \frac{1}{\tan}$.
For the two acute angles of a right triangle, $A + B = 90^\circ$ and $\sin A = \cos B$, since opposite and adjacent swap.
$\sin^2 + \cos^2 = \frac{a^2 + b^2}{c^2} = 1$, by the Pythagorean theorem.
The diagonal of a square bisects its right angles, giving a $45^\circ$-$45^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangle with equal legs.
A $45^\circ$-$45^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangle with legs $a$ has hypotenuse $a\sqrt{2}$.
$\sin 45^\circ = \cos 45^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ and $\tan 45^\circ = 1$, whatever the size.
The altitude of an equilateral triangle splits it into two congruent $30^\circ$-$60^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangles.
A $30^\circ$-$60^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangle has sides in the ratio $1 : \sqrt{3} : 2$.
The hypotenuse is twice the side opposite $30^\circ$.
So $\sin 30^\circ = \cos 60^\circ = \frac12$ and $\sin 60^\circ = \cos 30^\circ = \frac{\sqrt3}{2}$.
With hypotenuse $1$, the opposite leg is $\sin\theta$ and the adjacent leg is $\cos\theta$.
The exact values of all six ratios at $0^\circ$, $30^\circ$, $45^\circ$, $60^\circ$ and $90^\circ$.
$\sin 0^\circ = 0$ and $\cos 90^\circ = 0$, while $\tan 90^\circ$ is undefined because it would divide by zero.
With hypotenuse $1$, the legs are $\sin A$ and $\cos A$.
Cofunction identities: $\sin(90^\circ - A) = \cos A$ and $\cos(90^\circ - A) = \sin A$; likewise $\tan$ pairs with $\cot$ and $\sec$ with $\csc$.
Pythagorean identity: $\sin^2 A + \cos^2 A = 1$.
Dividing by $\cos^2 A$ gives $\tan^2 A + 1 = \sec^2 A$.
Dividing by $\sin^2 A$ gives $1 + \cot^2 A = \csc^2 A$.
The area of a triangle is $\frac12 bh$, where $h$ is the perpendicular from the opposite vertex to the line of the base $b$.
A right triangle is half a rectangle, so its area is half the product of its legs.
The proof splits the triangle by the altitude into two right triangles whose areas add (foot inside the base) or subtract (foot on the extension).
Any side can serve as the base; all three base-height products give the same area.
The area of a triangle is $\frac12 ab \sin C$, where $C$ is the angle between sides $a$ and $b$.
The altitude onto $a$ is $h = b \sin C$.
An angle and its supplement have the same sine, $\sin(180^\circ - C) = \sin C$, so the formula holds for obtuse $C$ too.
An equilateral triangle of side $s$ has area $\frac{\sqrt3}{4}s^2$.
The area of a triangle equals $rs$, its inradius times its semiperimeter.

Proof: the incentre $I$ is at distance $r$ from every side, since a radius meets its tangent at a right angle, so joining $I$ to the vertices gives three triangles of areas $\frac12 ra$, $\frac12 rb$, $\frac12 rc$.
Rearranged, the inradius is $r = \text{Area}/s$.
A right angle can only lie opposite the longest side.
A triangle is right-angled exactly when its two smaller angles are complementary, adding to $90^\circ$.
With $c$ the longest side: $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$ for a right triangle, $a^2 + b^2 > c^2$ for an acute one, and $a^2 + b^2 < c^2$ for an obtuse one.
A triangle is right-angled exactly when the median to its longest side is half that side.
The third vertex lies on the circle with the longest side as diameter exactly when its angle is right; outside the circle the angle is acute, inside it is obtuse.
To find the ratios in which two cevians divide each other, draw a line through a division point parallel to a side, creating similar triangles.
With $AE : EB = 1 : 3$ and $CD : DB = 1 : 2$, the cevians $AD$ and $CE$ meet at $F$ with $\dfrac{AF}{FD} = 1$ and $\dfrac{EF}{FC} = \dfrac12$, whatever the triangle's shape.
In general, with $AE : EB = 1 : m$ and $CD : DB = 1 : n$, $\dfrac{AF}{FD} = \dfrac{n+1}{m}$ and $\dfrac{EF}{FC} = \dfrac{n}{m+1}$.
The four angles of any quadrilateral sum to $360^\circ$.
Proof: a diagonal cuts the quadrilateral into two triangles, each with angle sum $180^\circ$.
This holds for a concave quadrilateral too, with a reflex angle above $180^\circ$, cutting along the diagonal from the reflex corner.
The median of a trapezoid joins the midpoints of its legs.
The median is parallel to the two bases.
The median's length is the average of the bases: $XY = \tfrac12(AB + DC)$.
The area of a trapezoid is its median times its height: $XY \cdot h$.
In a trapezoid, equal legs, equal base angles and equal diagonals each imply the other two.
Equal legs: the altitudes $AX = BY$ give congruent right triangles $AXD \cong BYC$ (HL), so $\angle D = \angle C$ and $\angle A = \angle B$.
Equal legs give equal diagonals $AC = BD$, via congruent right triangles $AXC \cong BYD$ (LL).
Conversely, equal diagonals or equal base angles force equal legs.
A parallelogram is a quadrilateral whose opposite sides are parallel.
A diagonal splits it into two congruent triangles (ASA), so opposite sides are equal and opposite angles are equal.
Consecutive angles are supplementary: $\angle A + \angle B = 180^\circ$.
The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.
The area of a parallelogram is base times height: $bh$.
Sliding the top side along its line, with base and height fixed, does not change the area.
With sides $a$, $b$ and angle $B$ between them, $h = a\sin B$ and the area is $ab\sin B$.
With diagonals $d_1$, $d_2$ crossing at angle $\theta$, the area is $\tfrac12 d_1 d_2 \sin\theta$.
A rhombus is a quadrilateral with four equal sides.
Every rhombus is a parallelogram, so its diagonals bisect each other.
The diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular.
The area of a rhombus is $\tfrac12 d_1 d_2$.
Its side satisfies $s^2 = (\tfrac12 d_1)^2 + (\tfrac12 d_2)^2$.
A rectangle is a parallelogram with four right angles; its diagonals are equal: $AC = BD = \sqrt{l^2 + w^2}$.
A square is both a rectangle and a rhombus: its diagonals are equal, bisect each other and are perpendicular.
The diagonal of a square of side $s$ is $s\sqrt2$.
Joining the midpoints of a square's sides in order gives a square.
A quadrilateral whose diagonals bisect each other is a parallelogram.
If the diagonals bisect each other and are perpendicular, it is a rhombus.
If the diagonals bisect each other and are equal, it is a rectangle; all three conditions together give a square.
Perpendicular diagonals alone do not make a rhombus, but the area is still $\tfrac12 d_1 d_2$.
Varignon's theorem: the midpoints of the sides of any quadrilateral form a parallelogram.
Each side of the midpoint parallelogram is parallel to a diagonal of the quadrilateral and half as long.
The angle of the midpoint parallelogram equals the angle between the diagonals, so perpendicular diagonals give a rectangle.
The midpoint parallelogram has half the area of the quadrilateral.
From each vertex of an $n$-gon, $n - 3$ diagonals go out.
An $n$-gon has $\tfrac{n(n-3)}{2}$ diagonals: $n(n-3)$ counts each diagonal twice, once from each end.
The $n - 3$ diagonals from one vertex cut a convex $n$-gon into $n - 2$ triangles.
The interior angles of an $n$-gon sum to $180^\circ(n - 2)$, depending only on the number of sides.
An exterior angle of a polygon is the turn from one side to the next; it and the interior angle add to $180^\circ$.
The exterior angles of any convex polygon sum to $360^\circ$, whatever $n$ is.
Proof: $180^\circ n - 180^\circ(n - 2) = 360^\circ$; equivalently, shrinking the polygon to a point gathers the exterior angles into one full turn.
In a regular $n$-gon each interior angle is $\tfrac{180^\circ(n-2)}{n}$ and each exterior angle is $\tfrac{360^\circ}{n}$.
A regular polygon has a centre $O$ at distance $R$ (the circumradius) from every vertex and $r$ (the apothem) from every side, meeting each side at its midpoint at a right angle.
Radii and apothems cut it into $2n$ congruent right triangles with angle $\theta = \tfrac{180^\circ}{n}$ at $O$.
With side $l$: $\tan\theta = \tfrac{l/2}{r}$ and $\sin\theta = \tfrac{l/2}{R}$.
The area of a regular polygon is half the perimeter times the apothem: $\tfrac12 (nl) r$.
A regular hexagon splits into six equilateral triangles from its centre, so its circumradius equals its side: $R = s$.
The area of a regular hexagon is $\tfrac{3\sqrt3}{2}s^2$.
The long diagonal joining opposite vertices is $2s$.
The short diagonal is $s\sqrt3$.
Joining every other vertex gives an equilateral triangle.
Angle chasing: alternate between isosceles base angles and the exterior angle theorem, building angles $b$, $2b$, $3b$ along a chain of equal segments.
With four equal links $BQ = QP = PA = AC$ and $BA = BC$, the angle at $B$ is $\tfrac{180^\circ}{7}$.
With an equilateral triangle $ABE$ on side $AB$ of square $ABCD$, $AE = AD$, so triangle $AED$ is isosceles.
Triangle outside the square: $\angle EAD = 150^\circ$, $\angle AED = 15^\circ$, $\angle BED = 45^\circ$.
Triangle inside the square: $\angle EAD = 30^\circ$, $\angle AED = 75^\circ$, $\angle BED = 135^\circ$.
In quadrilateral $ABCD$, $\angle A + \angle D = 360^\circ - \angle B - \angle C$, even when $\angle A$ and $\angle D$ separately are unknown.
With $\angle A = 3x$ and $\angle D = 3y$ trisected, the trisectors meet at angles $\angle AED = 180^\circ - (x + y)$ and $\angle AFD = 180^\circ - 2(x + y)$, fixed by $\angle B$ and $\angle C$ alone.
In a similar copy with ratio $k$, every length is multiplied by $k$, including altitudes and radii.
Area multiplies two lengths, so scaling by $k$ multiplies area by $k^2$.
The medial triangle $DEF$ joins the midpoints of the sides of $ABC$.
Each side of $DEF$ is half the parallel side of $ABC$, so $DEF \sim ABC$ with $k = \tfrac12$.
$[DEF] = \tfrac14 [ABC]$.
The midpoints cut $ABC$ into four congruent triangles.
Triangles with the same altitude have areas in the ratio of their bases: $[ABD] : [ADC] = BD : DC$.
Moving a vertex along a line parallel to the base does not change a triangle's area.
Triangles on the same base have areas in the ratio of their altitudes.
A median splits a triangle into two triangles of equal area.
The three medians cut a triangle into six triangles of equal area, each $\tfrac16 [ABC]$.
Proof: $GD = \tfrac13 AD$ at the centroid, so $[GCD] = \tfrac13 [ACD] = \tfrac16 [ABC]$.
The diagonals of trapezoid $ABCD$ ($AB \parallel DC$) make triangles $ABE \sim CDE$ by AA.
With $k = CD/AB$, $[CDE] = k^2\,[ABE]$.
The two side triangles have equal areas: $[AED] = [BEC]$.
If diagonal $AC$ passes through the midpoint of diagonal $BD$, it splits the quadrilateral into two equal areas: $[ACB] = [ACD]$.
Area by subtraction: an awkward region is a simple shape with simple pieces removed, as a ring has area $\pi R^2 - \pi r^2$.
A regular octagon of side $s$ fits in a square of side $s(1 + \sqrt2)$ with four isosceles right corner triangles of legs $s/\sqrt2$.
The area of a regular octagon of side $s$ is $2(1+\sqrt2)\,s^2$.
Hippocrates' lune: the crescent between a semicircle on the hypotenuse of an isosceles right triangle and a quarter circle centred at the right angle has area equal to the triangle.
Crescent $= T + S - Q$, and the semicircle $S$ equals the quarter circle $Q$, both $\tfrac14\pi a^2$, so the crescent's area is $\tfrac12 a^2$ with no $\pi$.
Inclusion–exclusion: when pieces overlap, their total area counts the overlaps twice; subtract the region covered once to leave the overlaps.
Four inward semicircles on the sides of a square of side $s$ make four leaves of total area $\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - 1\right)s^2$.
A circular segment has area sector minus triangle.
A $60^\circ$ segment of radius $r$ has area $\tfrac16 \pi r^2 - \frac{\sqrt3}{4} r^2$.
Three circles of radius $r$ centred on a circle of radius $r$ make three leaves of total area $\left(\pi - \frac{3\sqrt3}{2}\right) r^2$, six segments.
A point has a Cartesian address $(x, y)$ and a polar address $(r, \theta)$: distance from the origin and angle from the positive $x$-axis.
The axes cut the plane into four quadrants, numbered counter-clockwise from the upper right; the signs of $x$ and $y$ say which one a point is in.
$x = $ constant is a vertical line and $y = $ constant a horizontal one; $r = $ constant is a circle about the origin and $\theta = $ constant a ray.
$x = r\cos\theta$, $y = r\sin\theta$ and $r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$.
The slope of a line is rise over run, $m = \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}}$, and measures its steepness.
A line rising to the right has positive slope, a falling one negative slope, a horizontal one slope $0$, and a vertical line has undefined slope.
Any two points on a line give the same slope, because their rise–run triangles are similar.
A line with slope $m$ and $y$-intercept $b$ has equation $y = mx + b$.
The $y$-intercept is found by setting $x = 0$, the $x$-intercept by solving $0 = mx + b$; a horizontal line has no $x$-intercept.
Standard form writes a line as $Ax + By = C$ with whole numbers and $A \ge 0$; its slope is $-A/B$.
Through two points, $m$ is their rise over run and $b = y - mx$ from either point.
Parallel lines have equal slopes, $m_1 = m_2$.
Turning a line a quarter turn changes slope $\frac{a}{b}$ to $\frac{b}{-a}$.
Two lines with slopes are perpendicular exactly when $m_1 m_2 = -1$.
A horizontal and a vertical line are perpendicular, but the product rule does not apply since the vertical slope does not exist.
The segment $AB$ is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs $x_2 - x_1$ and $y_2 - y_1$.
The order of the points does not matter, since squaring removes the signs.
The midpoint of $AB$ is the average of the endpoints: $M = \left(\frac{x_1 + x_2}{2}, \frac{y_1 + y_2}{2}\right)$.
The point a fraction $t$ of the way from $A$ to $B$ is $(x_1 + t(x_2 - x_1),\ y_1 + t(y_2 - y_1))$.
These follow from similar right triangles along $AB$, congruent at the midpoint.
A circle is every point at distance $R$ from its centre $(p, q)$.
Its equation is $(x - p)^2 + (y - q)^2 = R^2$; the left side is less than $R^2$ inside, equal on, and greater outside the circle.
Expanded, it reads $x^2 + y^2 + Ax + By + C = 0$ with $A = -2p$, $B = -2q$, $C = p^2 + q^2 - R^2$.
Completing the square recovers the centre $(-\tfrac A2, -\tfrac B2)$ and $R^2 = \tfrac{A^2}{4} + \tfrac{B^2}{4} - C$.
A line and a circle meet in $2$, $1$ or $0$ points; meeting in exactly one means the line is tangent.
Substituting the line's equation into the circle's leaves a quadratic in one variable.
Its discriminant $D = b^2 - 4ac$ counts the meeting points: two if $D > 0$, one if $D = 0$, none if $D < 0$.
Two distinct lines share one point or none (if parallel); two circles share $0$, $1$ or $2$ points, since subtracting their equations leaves a line.
The three medians of a triangle meet at one point, the centroid $G$, shown by intersecting their line equations.
The centroid is the average of the three vertices: $G = \left(\frac{x_A + x_B + x_C}{3}, \frac{y_A + y_B + y_C}{3}\right)$.
$G$ divides each median two to one from the vertex: $AG = 2\,GD$.
Placing a triangle conveniently on the axes loses no generality, because moving the axes changes points and their averages by the same rule.
A solution of $ax + b = cx + d$ is an $x$ where the two sides are equal: where their lines cross.
Adding, subtracting, or dividing both sides by the same nonzero amount keeps the solutions unchanged.
Gathering $x$ terms and dividing gives $x = \frac{d - b}{a - c}$.
Check a solution by substituting it into the original equation.
If $a = c$ there is no solution unless $d = b$, when every $x$ works.
A linear equation in two unknowns, such as $x + y = 3$, has infinitely many solutions, which together form a straight line.
Solving for $y$ gives exactly one $y$ for each $x$, changing at a steady rate.
The degree of a term is the sum of its variables' powers; an equation is linear when it has degree $1$.
Only linear equations have solution sets that are lines; $xy = 4$ or $x^2 + y = 4$ give curves.
A solution of a system of two equations lies on both lines, so it is where they cross.
Substitution: solve one equation for one variable, substitute into the other, solve the resulting one-unknown equation, then go back for the other variable.
Check the pair in both original equations.
If the lines are parallel, substitution ends in a false statement like $0 = 3$ and there is no solution.
Multiplying an equation by a nonzero number does not change its solutions.
A sum of multiples of two equations is satisfied by any common solution, so its line passes through the crossing.
Elimination: scale the equations so one variable's coefficients cancel when added, solve for the other, then substitute back.
If elimination leaves $0 = $ a nonzero number the system has no solution (parallel lines); if it leaves $0 = 0$ the equations describe the same line and have infinitely many solutions.
At a steady rate, distance $=$ rate $\times$ time, $d = rt$: a straight line on a distance–time graph whose slope is the speed.
A start delayed by $h$ gives $d = r_2(t - h)$.
Two movers meet when their distances are equal; $r_1 t = r_2(t - h)$ gives $t = \frac{r_2 h}{r_2 - r_1}$.
Equal speeds give parallel lines and no meeting; check that an answer makes sense, such as rejecting a negative time.
Average speed is total distance divided by total time: the slope of the chord from start to finish.
Over equal distances at two speeds, the average speed is not the average of the speeds; the slower speed weighs more because more time is spent at it.
For equal distances there and back, the average speed is $\frac{2}{1/r_1 + 1/r_2}$, independent of the distance.
A job done alone in $a$ hours has rate $\frac{1}{a}$ of the job per hour.
Rates of working together add: $\frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b}$.
Together the job takes $t = \frac{1}{1/a + 1/b} = \frac{ab}{a + b}$.
A missing rate is a difference: $\frac{1}{b} = \frac{1}{t} - \frac{1}{a}$; this is rate $\times$ time $=$ distance with work in place of distance.
At a steady speed, height is linear in time: $h = H - vt$.
Under gravity, height in feet is $h = H - vt - 16t^2$, a curve.
Finding when it lands means solving $16t^2 + vt - H = 0$, an equation of degree two that the linear moves cannot solve.
Zero-product property: a product is zero only when one of its factors is zero, so $a(x - r)(x - s) = 0$ exactly when $x = r$ or $x = s$.
$(x - r)(x - s) = x^2 - (r + s)x + rs$: the $x$ coefficient is minus the sum of the roots, the constant their product.
To factor $x^2 + bx + c$, find two numbers with sum $-b$ and product $c$; positive $c$ means the roots share a sign.
Special shapes: a root at $0$ gives a factor $x$; $x^2 - r^2 = (x - r)(x + r)$; a double root gives a perfect square $(x - r)^2$, whose graph only touches the axis.
$x^2 + bx + \left(\frac{b}{2}\right)^2 = \left(x + \frac{b}{2}\right)^2$: to complete the square, halve the $x$ coefficient and square it.
To solve $x^2 + bx = k$, add $\left(\frac{b}{2}\right)^2$ to both sides and take a square root: $x = -\frac{b}{2} \pm \sqrt{k + \left(\frac{b}{2}\right)^2}$.
With a leading coefficient $a$, divide by $a$ first.
Every parabola $y = ax^2 + bx + c$ is symmetric about $x = -\frac{b}{2a}$, so its roots sit equally either side of that line.
Completing the square gives the quadratic formula $x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$.
The discriminant $D = b^2 - 4ac$ decides: two real roots if $D > 0$, a double root if $D = 0$, no real roots if $D < 0$.
With $D < 0$ the roots are complex conjugates $-\frac{b}{2a} \pm i\frac{\sqrt{-D}}{2a}$; with whole-number coefficients an irrational root $p + \sqrt{q}$ comes paired with $p - \sqrt{q}$.
Sum and product of roots: $r + s = -\frac{b}{a}$ and $rs = \frac{c}{a}$.
Squaring both sides of $\sqrt{x + p} = x + q$ gives a quadratic, $x + p = (x + q)^2$.
Squaring can introduce extraneous roots: solutions of the squared equation that fail the original, since it cannot tell $\sqrt{x + p}$ from $-\sqrt{x + p}$.
Always check every root in the original equation; $\sqrt{\ }$ means the positive root.
Multiplying through by an expression in $x$ can also add roots: discard any that make that expression zero.
An equation in an expression and its square, such as $x^4 + Bx^2 + C = 0$, becomes a quadratic $z^2 + Bz + C = 0$ by substituting $z = x^2$.
Solve for $z$, then undo the substitution: a positive $z$ gives $x = \pm\sqrt{z}$, $z = 0$ gives $x = 0$, and a negative $z$ gives only complex $x = \pm i\sqrt{-z}$.
Other disguises work the same way, such as $z = 2^n$ in $2^{2n} - 6 \cdot 2^n + 8 = 0$; discard values of $z$ the substitution cannot take.
The trick fails if an extra term, such as $x$ in $x^4 + x^2 + x$, is not a power of the substituted expression.
A polynomial with roots $r_1, r_2, \ldots$ is the product $(x - r_1)(x - r_2)\cdots$, zero exactly at its roots.
At a simple root the graph changes sign; at a double root it touches the axis and turns away.
A cubic is $x^3 - (r_1 + r_2 + r_3)x^2 + (r_1r_2 + r_1r_3 + r_2r_3)x - r_1r_2r_3$: the coefficients hold the roots' sums and products with alternating signs.
A polynomial has as many roots as its degree; those not on the axis are complex, in conjugate pairs, so a cubic always has at least one real root.
When two chords $AB$ and $CD$ cross at $E$ inside a circle, $AE \cdot EB = CE \cdot ED$.
Proof: triangles $EAC$ and $EDB$ have equal vertical angles at $E$ and equal inscribed angles on the same arc, so $\triangle EAC \sim \triangle EDB$.
The equal ratios $\dfrac{AE}{DE} = \dfrac{CE}{BE}$ cross-multiply into the equal products.
From an outside point $P$, with tangent $PT$ and a secant meeting the circle at $A$ and $B$: $PT^2 = PA \cdot PB$.
Proof: $\triangle PTA \sim \triangle PBT$, since they share the angle at $P$ and the tangent–chord angle $\angle PTA$ equals the inscribed angle $\angle PBT$ on arc $TA$.
Any two secants from $P$ therefore give equal products: $PA \cdot PB = PC \cdot PD$.
The two tangent segments from a point $P$ outside a circle are equal: $PS = PT$.
The line $PO$ to the centre bisects the angle between the two tangents.
Proof: the radii $OS$ and $OT$ meet the tangents at right angles, so right triangles $POS$ and $POT$ share hypotenuse $PO$ and have equal legs, and are congruent (HL).
Equivalently, each tangent squared equals the power $d^2 - r^2$, where $d = PO$.
For a point $P$ and any line through it meeting the circle at $A$ and $B$, the product $PA \cdot PB$ is the same for every line: the power of the point.
With $d = OP$ and radius $r$, the power is $PA \cdot PB = |d^2 - r^2|$, read off the line through the centre.
Outside the circle the tangent gives $PT^2 = d^2 - r^2$; inside, the chord perpendicular to $OP$ is halved at $P$ and its half $h$ has $h^2 = r^2 - d^2$.
On the circle the power is zero.
The incircle cuts the sides into tangent lengths that pair up by corner: $x$ at $A$, $y$ at $B$, $z$ at $C$, with $a = y + z$, $b = z + x$, $c = x + y$.
The semiperimeter is $s = x + y + z$.
Each tangent length is $s$ minus the opposite side: $x = s - a$, $y = s - b$, $z = s - c$.
In a right triangle with the right angle at $C$, the inradius is $r = s - c = \tfrac12(a + b - c)$.
In a quadrilateral with an inscribed circle, the sums of opposite sides are equal: $AB + CD = BC + DA$.
Proof: each corner sends two equal tangents $w, x, y, z$ to the circle, and each pair of opposite sides is made of one tangent from every corner, $w + x + y + z$.
A line can lie in a plane, pierce it at exactly one point, or never meet it, when it is parallel to the plane.
A line is perpendicular to a plane only if it is perpendicular to every line of the plane through its foot; one right angle is not enough.
The distance from a point $P$ to a plane is the perpendicular segment $PH$; any slanted segment $PF$ is the hypotenuse of right triangle $PHF$ and so is longer.
Two lines in space are parallel if they point the same way; lines that point different ways and never meet are skew.
A plane cuts a sphere in a circle; when the plane passes through the centre the cut is a great circle.
The segment from the sphere's centre $O$ to the centre $B$ of the cut is perpendicular to the plane (by SSS congruent triangles $OBA$ and $OBC$).
A plane at distance $d$ from the centre of a sphere of radius $r$ cuts a circle of radius $\sqrt{r^2 - d^2}$.
A cube of edge $s$ has surface area $6s^2$ and volume $s^3$.
The face diagonal of a cube is $s\sqrt2$.
The space diagonal of a cube is $s\sqrt3$, from right triangle $ACG$ with $AG^2 = 2s^2 + s^2$.
The three face diagonals joining the corners next to one corner form an equilateral triangle of side $s\sqrt2$.
The midpoints of the three edges at a corner form an equilateral triangle of side $\tfrac{s\sqrt2}{2}$.
The floor diagonal of an $l \times w \times h$ box satisfies $AC^2 = l^2 + w^2$.
A vertical edge is perpendicular to every line in the floor through its foot, so $ACG$ is a right triangle.
The space diagonal of a box is $\sqrt{l^2 + w^2 + h^2}$, by Pythagoras twice.
A painted cube of edge $n$ cut into $n^3$ unit blocks has $8$ blocks with three painted faces (the corners).
It has $12(n - 2)$ blocks with two painted faces (along the edges) and $6(n - 2)^2$ with one (inside the faces).
It has $(n - 2)^3$ unpainted blocks inside, and the four counts add up to $n^3$.
The volume of a prism or cylinder is base area times height: $V = Bh$.
The lateral surface of a right prism unrolls into one rectangle, so its area is $ph$: perimeter times height.
A cylinder's wall unrolls into a $2\pi r$ by $h$ rectangle, so its lateral area is $2\pi rh$; add two discs for the total surface.
The shortest path over a curved wall is a straight line on the unrolled rectangle; from a top point to the opposite bottom point it is $\sqrt{h^2 + (\pi r)^2}$.
In a regular pyramid the base is a regular polygon and the apex lies directly above its centre, so the side faces are congruent triangles.
Every pyramid has volume $V = \tfrac13 Bh$, a third of the prism on the same base with the same height.
A cube splits into three congruent pyramids with base $c^2$ and height $c$, each of volume $\tfrac13 c^3$.
The slant height $l = PM$ is the altitude of a side face, with $PM^2 = PO^2 + OM^2$.
The lateral area of a regular pyramid is $\tfrac12 pl$, with $p$ the base perimeter.
A cone has volume $V = \tfrac13 \pi r^2 h$, a third of the cylinder around it.
The slant height $l$ of a right circular cone satisfies $r^2 + h^2 = l^2$.
The lateral surface unrolls into a sector of radius $l$ whose arc has length $2\pi r$, the fraction $\tfrac{r}{l}$ of the full circle.
The lateral area of a cone is $\pi r l$ and its total surface area is $\pi r l + \pi r^2$.
A regular tetrahedron is a pyramid whose four faces are equilateral triangles of side $s$.
Its altitude lands on the centroid $G$ of the base, since $GA = GB = GC$ by congruent right triangles.
$AG = \tfrac23 \cdot \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}s = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{3}s$, so the height is $DG = \tfrac{\sqrt6}{3}s$.
The volume of a regular tetrahedron is $V = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{12}s^3$.
A regular octahedron has eight equilateral faces, four meeting at each corner.
Its middle square of side $s$ splits it into two congruent square pyramids.
Each pyramid has height $PO = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}s$, equal to half the square's diagonal.
The volume of a regular octahedron is $V = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{3}s^3$.
A regular polyhedron has every face the same regular polygon and every corner alike; there are exactly five.
With $p$-sided faces and $q$ faces at each corner, $E = \tfrac{pF}{2}$ and $V = \tfrac{pF}{q}$.
Euler's formula $V - E + F = 2$ holds for every convex polyhedron.
The face angles at a corner must total less than $360^\circ$, which allows only 3, 4 or 5 triangles, 3 squares, or 3 pentagons.
A translation moves every point by the same arrow: $(x, y) \to (x + a, y + b)$.
Since $AA'$ and $BB'$ are equal and parallel, $ABB'A'$ is a parallelogram, so each image side is equal and parallel to its original.
The image is congruent and has the same orientation.
A translation other than the zero slide fixes no point.
A rotation about $O$ through $\theta$ keeps each point's distance from $O$ and turns it through $\theta$: $OB = OB'$ and $\angle BOB' = \theta$; only $O$ is fixed.
The image is congruent, and a line and its image cross at the angle of rotation $\theta$.
A rotation sends collinear points to collinear points, proved with SAS congruent triangles sharing the vertex $O$.
In a reflection the mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining each point to its image; points on the mirror are fixed.
A reflection keeps lengths, so the image is congruent, but it reverses orientation.
A line and its image meet on the mirror and make equal angles with it.
Reflection in a point $O$ sends each point through $O$ to the same distance on the other side, so $O$ is the midpoint of every segment $AA'$.
In coordinates, $A' = O + (O - A) = 2O - A$.
Reflection in a point is the same map as a half-turn ($180^\circ$ rotation) about it.
A distortion (one-way stretch) multiplies every point's distance from a fixed line by $k$ and leaves the other coordinate unchanged.
It sends lines to lines but changes angles, so the image is generally not similar; a circle becomes an ellipse.
A distortion with factor $k$ multiplies every area by $k$, since each thin strip along the stretch has its length multiplied by $k$.
A dilation with centre $O$ and factor $k$ sends $A$ to $A'$ on line $OA$ with $OA' = |k| \cdot OA$, on $A$'s side when $k > 0$ and the opposite side when $k < 0$.
Lines through matching points all pass through the centre $O$.
By SAS similarity $\triangle OAB \sim \triangle OA'B'$, so $A'B' = |k| \cdot AB$ and $A'B' \parallel AB$.
The image is similar to the original and its area is multiplied by $k^2$.
Translations, rotations and reflections are rigid motions: they keep lengths, angles and area, so the image is congruent.
Of the rigid motions, only a reflection reverses orientation.
A dilation changes lengths and area but keeps angles, so the image is similar.
A distortion keeps neither lengths nor angles, but like all five transformations it sends straight lines to straight lines.
A regular $n$-gon has $n$ rotational symmetries, the multiples of $360^\circ / n$, counting the turn of $0^\circ$.
A regular $n$-gon has $n$ mirror lines, each through a corner or the midpoint of a side.
A regular $n$-gon has point symmetry (a half-turn symmetry) exactly when $n$ is even.
To find the shortest path from $A$ to a line and on to $B$ (same side), reflect $B$ in the line to $B'$; then $PB = PB'$ for every $P$ on the line.
By the triangle inequality $AP + PB' \ge AB'$, so the best point $P^*$ is where segment $AB'$ crosses the line, and the shortest trip has length $AB'$.
The shortest path meets the line at equal angles, like light off a mirror.
The radii to the ends of a common tangent are both perpendicular to it, hence parallel.
For two circles with radii $R$, $r$ and centres $d$ apart, the common tangent length is $t = \sqrt{d^2 - (R - r)^2}$ for an open belt and $t = \sqrt{d^2 - (R + r)^2}$ for a crossed belt.
With $\cos\alpha = O_1H / d$, the open belt hugs $2\pi - 2\alpha$ of the big wheel and $2\alpha$ of the small one; the crossed belt hugs $2\pi - 2\alpha$ of each.
An arc of angle $\theta$ radians on radius $\rho$ has length $\rho\theta$, so the belt length is two tangents plus two arcs.
The bisector of angle $A$ meets the circumcircle again at $D$, the midpoint of arc $BC$, so $DB = DC$.
Equal inscribed angles cut off equal arcs, and equal arcs have equal chords.
With incentre $I$, $\angle DBI = \angle BID = \alpha + \beta$, so triangle $DBI$ is isosceles.
$DB = DI = DC$, so the circle centred at $D$ passes through $B$, $I$ and $C$.
The common chord of two overlapping circles cuts their lens into two circular segments.
A circular segment is a sector minus a triangle: with central angle $\theta$ in radians, its area is $\tfrac12 R^2(\theta - \sin\theta)$.
The lens area is $\tfrac12 R_1^2(\theta_1 - \sin\theta_1) + \tfrac12 R_2^2(\theta_2 - \sin\theta_2)$.
A fold is a reflection in the crease, so the crease that takes $A$ to $A'$ is the perpendicular bisector of $AA'$.
A fold keeps lengths and angles, so the flap is congruent to the region it came from and $EA = EA'$, $FA = FA'$.
Folding the corner of a sheet of width $w$ onto the far side at distance $t$ from corner $B$: $x^2 = (w - x)^2 + t^2$, so $x = \frac{w^2 + t^2}{2w}$.
Viviani's theorem: from any point inside an equilateral triangle, the perpendicular distances to the three sides add up to the altitude: $d_1 + d_2 + d_3 = h$.
Proof: joining the point to the vertices makes three triangles on bases $s$, so $\tfrac12 s d_1 + \tfrac12 s d_2 + \tfrac12 s d_3 = \tfrac12 s h$.
An equilateral triangle of side $s$ has altitude $h = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}s$ and area $\tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}s^2$.
Crossed ladders: lines from the tops of posts of heights $x$ and $y$ to the foot of the other cross at height $z$ with $\dfrac1x + \dfrac1y = \dfrac1z$.
Proof: two pairs of similar right triangles give $\dfrac{z}{x} = \dfrac{n}{m + n}$ and $\dfrac{z}{y} = \dfrac{m}{m + n}$, which add to $1$.
The crossing height does not depend on the distance between the posts.
